title: Genesis 36:20–43
context: The chapter turns to Seir’s Horite inhabitants, then to Anah who found hot springs, Horite chiefs, and the kings who reigned in Edom before any king reigned over Israel. It closes with Esau’s chiefs listed by clans and dwelling places—Edom’s real geography under God’s care.

voices.heading: Voices from both camps
voices.intro: Historic words on Horite chiefs and kings in Edom before any king in Israel—so each camp speaks in its own voice beside Genesis 36:20–43.
voices.note: Quotations lightly abridged for length; wording follows standard English translations of the sources named.

arminian.quote: These are the sons of Seir—In the midst of the genealogy of the Edomites is inserted the genealogy of the Horites, those Canaanites, or Hittites, (compare Gen 26:34,) that were the natives of mount Seir. Mention is made of them, Gen 14:6, and of their interest in mount Seir before the Edomites took possession of it, Deu 2:12,22. This comes in here, not only to give light to the story, but to be a standing reflexion upon the Edomites for intermarrying with them, by which it is likely they learned their way, and corrupted themselves.
arminian.source: Explanatory Notes upon the Old Testament (on Gen 36:20)

reformed.quote: These are the kings that reigned, etc We must keep in memory what we have said a little before, that reprobates are suddenly exalted, that they may immediately fall, like the herb upon the roofs, which is destitute of root, and has a hasty growth, but withers the more quickly. To the two sons of Isaac had been promised the honor that kings should spring from them.

verses.text: These are the sons of Seir the Horite, the inhabitants of the land: Lotan, Shobal, Zibeon, Anah,
verses.arminianNotes:
New heading: sons of Seir the Horite, inhabitants of the land. Before Edom’s kings, the text honors the people already in Seir.

Classical Arminians refuse to skip Horites as extras. God names prior inhabitants because they were truly there.
verses.reformedNotes:
Horites are “inhabitants of the land”—Seir was not empty. God records the people Deuteronomy will later say Esau dispossessed (Deut 2:12, 22).

Providence over territories includes those who dwelt there first.

verses.text: Dishon, Ezer, and Dishan; these are the chiefs of the Horites, the sons of Seir in the land of Edom.
verses.arminianNotes:
Dishon, Ezer, and Dishan complete Seir’s seven sons, called chiefs of the Horites in Edom’s land. Two similar names (Dishon/Dishan) are kept distinct.

The land can hold both Horite chiefs and, in time, Edomite ones.
verses.reformedNotes:
Seven Horite chiefs in the land of Edom. God numbers Seir’s house as carefully as Esau’s.

Reformed reading: the stage of Edom was already peopled; the Lord ordered both occupancy and later displacement without fictionalizing the Horites.

verses.text: The sons of Lotan were Hori and Hemam; and Lotan’s sister was Timna.
verses.arminianNotes:
Lotan’s sons Hori and Hemam; Lotan’s sister Timna. The Timna of v. 12 now has a Horite brother—kinship across the two lists.

God lets a sister’s name explain a concubine in Esau’s house. Intermarriage is reported, not sneered at.
verses.reformedNotes:
Timna’s Horite identity ties Amalek’s mother to Seir. Providence knits the inhabitant line to Eliphaz.

The sister is named because the Lord of genealogies does not hide the join.

verses.text: These are the sons of Shobal: Alvan, Manahath, Ebal, Shepho, and Onam.
verses.arminianNotes:
Shobal’s sons: Alvan, Manahath, Ebal, Shepho, Onam. Five Horite names with the same dignity as Japheth’s grandsons in chapter 10.

Wideness of care: God knows clans Israel will barely meet.
verses.reformedNotes:
Another Horite pentad. God is mapping Seir clan by clan.

These names exist in Scripture because He willed their memory.

verses.text: These are the sons of Zibeon: Aiah and Anah; he is the Anah who found the hot springs in the wilderness, as he pastured the donkeys of Zibeon his father.
verses.arminianNotes:
Zibeon’s sons Aiah and Anah—and a narrative pause: this Anah found the hot springs in the wilderness while pasturing his father’s donkeys.

The Bible is not too holy for a herder’s discovery. Common life in Seir is worth a sentence.
verses.reformedNotes:
Anah is identified by a wilderness find and ordinary work. God records a Horite anecdote as true history.

Providence includes hot springs and donkeys, not only thrones.

verses.text: These are the children of Anah: Dishon and Oholibamah the daughter of Anah.
verses.arminianNotes:
Anah’s children: Dishon and Oholibamah his daughter. The wife of Esau (vv. 2, 14, 18) is here a Horite daughter.

Family ties between Esau and Seir are on the page for anyone willing to read slowly.
verses.reformedNotes:
Oholibamah named from her father’s house. The marriage that linked Esau to the inhabitants is genealogically pinned.

God wanted that pin in both lists.

verses.text: These are the sons of Dishon: Hemdan, Eshban, Ithran, and Cheran.
verses.arminianNotes:
Dishon’s sons: Hemdan, Eshban, Ithran, Cheran. Four more Horite names, unmocked.

Arminian pastoral: being briefly listed is still being known by God.
verses.reformedNotes:
Dishon’s house is filled out. The Lord counts Seir’s grandsons.

No scorn for a list without stories.

verses.text: These are the sons of Ezer: Bilhan, Zaavan, and Akan.
verses.arminianNotes:
Ezer’s sons: Bilhan, Zaavan, Akan. Three names, same care.

Peoples on the edge of Israel’s memory still belong to the God of all nations.
verses.reformedNotes:
Ezer’s three take their row. Providence is not in a hurry to reach the kings.

The Horite table must be complete first.

verses.text: These are the sons of Dishan: Uz and Aran.
verses.arminianNotes:
Dishan’s sons: Uz and Aran. Uz elsewhere names lands; here it is a Horite grandson.

God can reuse names across tables without confusion in His own mind.
verses.reformedNotes:
Dishan, distinct from Dishon, receives two sons. The spelling difference is kept.

Reformed note: precision in the Horite list is a kind of reverence for God’s bookkeeping.

verses.text: These are the chiefs of the Horites: the chiefs Lotan, Shobal, Zibeon, Anah,
verses.arminianNotes:
Horite chiefs restated: Lotan, Shobal, Zibeon, Anah. Sons become titled heads, as Esau’s sons did.

Common-grace government is not Israel’s monopoly.
verses.reformedNotes:
The chief-list mirrors v. 20. God confirms Horite polity in Seir.

Structure is given, not invented as a joke at genealogy’s expense.

verses.text: Dishon, Ezer, and Dishan; these are the chiefs of the Horites, chief by chief in the land of Seir.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Chief by chief in the land of Seir” slows the reader to take each head seriously.

Arminians hear honor: Seir had a constitution before Edom’s kings are named.
verses.reformedNotes:
“Chief by chief” is deliberate pacing. The land of Seir had ordered leadership under God’s allotment.

Only then does the narrator turn to kings.

verses.text: These are the kings who reigned in the land of Edom, before any king reigned over the Israelites.
verses.arminianNotes:
Kings in Edom before any king reigned over the Israelites. The note is historical, not a taunt: Edom’s monarchy is earlier, and Scripture tells the truth.

Classical Arminians hear God sincerely governing all peoples. Israel’s later kingship is not the only throne God noticed; Edom’s royal list honors real politics outside the chosen line.
verses.reformedNotes:
The narrator timestamps Edom’s kings against Israel’s then-future monarchy. God orders nations on different clocks.

Reformed confession: Edom’s earlier kings still sit inside His purpose with Jacob. The delay of Israel’s king is not because God forgot His people; it is His timing—and Edom’s throne is recorded without being baptized as the covenant kingship.
verses.keyContrast: Both take v. 31 as sober history, not mockery of genealogies or of Edom. Arminians typically stress that God sincerely governs and honestly records all peoples’ kings; Reformed readers typically stress that God sovereignly sequences the nations—Edom’s earlier monarchy still serves His covenant purpose with Jacob without erasing Esau’s royal posterity.

verses.text: Bela the son of Beor reigned in Edom, the name of his city being Dinhabah.
verses.arminianNotes:
Bela son of Beor, city Dinhabah. First named king of Edom, with a capital.

A city and a father: Edom’s throne begins in particulars.
verses.reformedNotes:
The king-list opens like any royal chronicle God is willing to preserve. Bela of Dinhabah is not a myth the narrator needed.

Providence over Edom’s first crown.

verses.text: Bela died, and Jobab the son of Zerah of Bozrah reigned in his place.
verses.arminianNotes:
Bela dies; Jobab son of Zerah of Bozrah reigns. Succession by death, a new city (Bozrah, later famed in prophecy).

Thrones pass. God records Edom’s ordinary royal mortality.
verses.reformedNotes:
Death and replacement: Edom’s kings are mortal under the same Lord. Bozrah enters the map because God placed a king there.

The list’s “in his place” is providence, not chance.

verses.text: Jobab died, and Husham of the land of the Temanites reigned in his place.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jobab dies; Husham of the Temanites reigns. Teman, already a clan name, now a royal catchment.

Regions of Edom take turns on the throne—real local identity.
verses.reformedNotes:
A Temanite king means Eliphaz’s famous branch can yield a crown. God ties the king-list back to the clan-list.

Geography and dynasty meet under His rule.

verses.text: Husham died, and Hadad the son of Bedad, who defeated Midian in the country of Moab, reigned in his place, the name of his city being Avith.
verses.arminianNotes:
Husham dies; Hadad son of Bedad, who defeated Midian in Moab, reigns from Avith. One king has a deed, not only a name.

Arminian reading: Edomite military history is allowed on the page. God does not reduce every foreign victory to a footnote of Israel.
verses.reformedNotes:
A Midian-defeating Hadad is remembered with his city. God superintends wars east of the Jordan even when Israel has no king yet.

The deed sits in Edom’s chronicle because the Lord of hosts is Lord there too.

verses.text: Hadad died, and Samlah of Masrekah reigned in his place.
verses.arminianNotes:
Hadad dies; Samlah of Masrekah reigns. Another city, another name, no extra tale.

Brief notices still honor a real reign.
verses.reformedNotes:
Masrekah’s Samlah is a full row in God’s book. Silence about exploits is not contempt.

The Lord numbers reigns He does not narrate at length.

verses.text: Samlah died, and Shaul of Rehoboth on the Euphrates reigned in his place.
verses.arminianNotes:
Samlah dies; Shaul of Rehoboth on the Euphrates (Hebrew: “the River”) reigns. Edom’s horizon can reach a riverine Rehoboth.

Nations have wide connections; the record is not embarrassed by them.
verses.reformedNotes:
Rehoboth-on-the-River is a geographic marker God kept. Whether one takes “the River” as the Euphrates, the point is an Edomite king with a named origin beyond a local village.

Providence stretches Edom’s royal map.

verses.text: Shaul died, and Baal-hanan the son of Achbor reigned in his place.
verses.arminianNotes:
Shaul dies; Baal-hanan son of Achbor reigns. A theophoric name with “Baal” is reported without panic or sneer.

The narrator can tell the truth about an Edomite name and still keep the man in the list.
verses.reformedNotes:
Baal-hanan son of Achbor: God records even names that may confess another worship. Common-grace kingship is not the same as covenant faith.

The throne in Edom remains under the Lord’s government.

verses.text: Baal-hanan the son of Achbor died, and Hadar reigned in his place, the name of his city being Pau; his wife’s name was Mehetabel, the daughter of Matred, daughter of Mezahab.
verses.arminianNotes:
Baal-hanan dies; Hadar reigns in Pau. Unusually, a queen-mother line is given: Mehetabel, daughter of Matred, daughter of Mezahab.

Women close the king-list. God is willing to name Edomite wives and grandmothers.
verses.reformedNotes:
Hadar of Pau, with Mehetabel’s pedigree. The extra names are not ornaments; they are history God preserved.

Reformed note: a foreign court gets a matriline in Holy Scripture because the Lord of nations keeps more than Israel’s family album.

verses.text: These are the names of the chiefs of Esau, according to their clans and their dwelling places, by their names: the chiefs Timna, Alvah, Jetheth,
verses.arminianNotes:
A final chief-list of Esau by clans, dwelling places, and names: Timna, Alvah, Jetheth. This roster is territorial as well as genealogical.

Places matter. God locates Edomite heads where they lived.
verses.reformedNotes:
Chiefs “according to their clans and their dwelling places.” Providence now maps Edom as land tenure, not only blood.

Timna as a chief-name may echo the earlier woman; God can reuse names in a people’s geography.

verses.text: Oholibamah, Elah, Pinon,
verses.arminianNotes:
Oholibamah, Elah, Pinon—three more chiefs, one sharing a wife’s name. Clans can carry a mother’s name into a district.

The list keeps Edom concrete.
verses.reformedNotes:
Pinon and Elah sit beside Oholibamah as territorial chiefs. God is closing the chapter with geography.

Dwelling places are part of the claim that Edom truly possessed a land.

verses.text: Kenaz, Teman, Mibzar,
verses.arminianNotes:
Kenaz, Teman, Mibzar—names already heard as sons now heard as places and chiefs. Continuity of clan and country.

God lets readers see the same Edom from two angles without despising either.
verses.reformedNotes:
Kenaz and Teman return as territorial titles. The double appearance is structure, not a slip.

The Lord who named sons now names seats.

verses.text: Magdiel, and Iram; these are the chiefs of Edom (that is, Esau, the father of Edom), according to their dwelling places in the land of their possession.
verses.arminianNotes:
Magdiel and Iram close the chiefs of Edom—that is, Esau, father of Edom—according to dwelling places in the land of their possession.

The last word is possession: Edom had a land. Classical Arminians hear God sincerely granting and recording a nation’s home outside Israel’s inheritance.
verses.reformedNotes:
The chapter ends as it began: Esau is Edom, now with chiefs in the land of their possession. Election of Jacob did not leave Esau landless in the narrator’s theology.

Reformed close: God ordered Edom’s holdings to serve His wider purpose with Israel—borders, later prophets, even Deuteronomy’s charge not to contend for Seir—while still telling the truth that the land was theirs.
